(3) The meniscus in this tank is pinned at the rim and set by over- or underfilling (angle δ), not a wall contact-angle meniscus. (4) Peak-or-peak-to-peak basis: the companion JFM paper defines 'the acceleration amplitude as A, which is the average min–max of a', which may mean peak-to-peak. checks.issue: All quotes found verbatim in the Exp. Fluids 62:59 PDF ('such a meniscus is needed...', 'g effectively becomes a time-varying value...', 'the greater the degree of under/overfilling...'). The glass-versus-plastic implication is the researcher's inference, not the paper's. The paper's menisci were pinned at the rim and set by fill volume, not by wall contact angle. The paper also says either curvature 'serves equally well', so polypropylene's 0.57 mm depression should still make rings. Only near-90° angles, such as polystyrene's 0.12 mm meniscus, suppress them.

checks.issue: Wilson et al. 2022 eq. (21) confirmed. My conversion to dimensional form is the same: ω² = (gk + σk³/ρ) tanh(kh). Karjanto eq. (5), ω² = gk tanh kh, confirmed. Aside: eq. (21) implies a decay rate of νk², half of Denner's 2νk²; this does not affect the dispersion relation.

Denner et al. quote confirmed: 'Γ = 2νk², applicable for k ≪ ω0/ν'. Wilson Table I water values confirmed: 71.6 mN/m, 0.96 mPa s, 997 kg/m³. Γ is an amplitude decay rate; energy decays at 4νk². The ignored wall and contact-line damping is correctly flagged.

Recomputed independently: k = 264.7, 526.4 and 906.4 /m; λ = 23.7, 11.9 and 6.9 mm; c_phase 23.7, 23.9 and 27.7 cm/s; c_group 20.0, 28.0 and 37.7 cm/s; decay lengths 1.48, 0.53 and 0.24 m; crossing 35 mm takes 0.09-0.18 s; l_c = 2.73 mm. All match.

Karjanto confirmed: 'maximum stroke |Sn| from an equilibrium position', 'approaching the asymptotic limit of Tn = 2 for kn0 h → ∞', 'This first-order theory can also be found in Dean and Dalrymple'. The ratio is for amplitude over displacement amplitude, so a = 2X is the right basis. Two problems. (1) The result is for gravity waves only (eq. 5 has no surface tension). At 20-40 Hz the ripples are capillary-dominated (k·l_c = 1.4-2.5), so the constant is being used outside its derivation. (2) The meniscus carried by the moving wall adds a source of the same order. Tilting effective gravity by Ẍ/g changes the wall meniscus height by about 3.6X at 20 Hz (θ = 20°); its radiated part is about 0.9X, with unknown phase. So the true ratio could plausibly be 1 to 3, and low_si = 1 is an unsourced assumption. As a sanity check, my 2D closed-tank solution reproduces the 2X scale, multiplied by a tan(kL) resonance factor.
checks.corrected: Status: verified for the value 2, with scope 'deep-water gravity waves, no surface tension'. Put the 1-3 range in a separate estimate for capillary ripples with a meniscus (Hocking & Mahdmina 1991, JFM 224, and Cocciaro et al. 1991 are relevant but were not fetched).

Quote confirmed verbatim, with 15-20 Hz peak sensitivity, about 60 Hz photopic cut-off and about 15 Hz at low light. One nuance on the implication: these are full-field flicker figures at maximum contrast. Long-exposure imaging blurs travelling waves out and shows only standing (resonant) patterns (Shao: 'traveling waves ... blurred over'). So in dim light a single footstep's travelling ripple may vanish rather than show a ring pattern.
checks.corrected: Soften the implication: 'in dim light, travelling ripples may blur away; only standing patterns stay visible'.

checks.issue: Recomputed. The side-to-side figures are right: 0.017-0.035, 0.017-0.035 and 0.020-0.040 mm/s. The up-and-down figures rest on the heuristic η = 1/√(1+(k·l_c)²), which overstates the radiated wave. I modelled vertical shaking as the surface pressure ρA·ζ0(x) acting on an exponential meniscus, used the linear capillary-gravity Green's function, and checked it by numerical inverse transform. The radiated amplitude is a = A·z_m·k·l_c/((1+(k·l_c)²)·ω·c_g). This reduces exactly to the researcher's quasi-static (A/2g)·z_m at the wall as ω → 0 (numerically 162 vs 159 µm per m/s²). The heuristic gives 1.1×, 2.2× and 5.2× too much wave at 10, 20 and 40 Hz. Corrected up-and-down PPV at 1 arcmin: 0.074-0.12, 0.053-0.088 and 0.056-0.093 mm/s (θ = 20-50°, free contact angle). The minimum is then 0.017, 0.017 and 0.020 mm/s, set by side-to-side at every frequency. The headline 0.02 mm/s survives. Status is wrong: the criterion 'acuity = detection threshold for a vibrating reflection' is an assumption, and it is not a true best case, because motion and vernier hyperacuity can go below 1 arcmin.

recommendation_issues:
1. **The up-and-down (meniscus) formula overstates the radiated wave.** It is PPV_v = a·2g/(z_m·η·ω), with η = 1/√(1+(k·l_c)²), and it overstates the wave by 1.1×, 2.2× and 5.2× at 10, 20 and 40 Hz.
   - Treat vertical shaking as the oscillating surface pressure ρA·z_m·e^(−x/l_c) on the meniscus. The linear capillary-gravity Green's function then gives a = A·z_m·k·l_c/((1+(k·l_c)²)·ω·c_g), with a free contact angle; multiply by about k·l_c for a pinned line.
   - So PPV_v = A/ω = a·c_g·(1+(k·l_c)²)/(z_m·k·l_c), with a = s/k.
   - I checked this by numerical inverse transform. It reduces exactly to the researcher's quasi-static (A/2g)·z_m at the wall as ω → 0.
   - It is still a small-slope model of a steep meniscus. Label it an estimate.

2. **The expected values change at 40 Hz.** They were 0.17, 0.17 and 0.11 mm/s. Corrected, they are 0.17, 0.17 and 0.20 mm/s. Side-to-side sets all three.
   - That threshold has a simple closed form: PPV_h = (θv/2)·c_phase/r. With c_phase near the 23-28 cm/s capillary-gravity minimum, this explains why it is flat with frequency. Use it directly.

3. **The concentric-ring threshold is higher than the shimmer threshold.** Rings (vertical) need about 0.5-1 mm/s at 10 arcmin.
   - The page wording ('Up-and-down shaking ... pump out rings, which is the Jurassic Park look' next to 0.2 mm/s) conflates the two.
   - Give two numbers, and compare horizontal ground PPV with 0.2 mm/s and vertical with about 0.5-1 mm/s. Taking 'the strongest single component' is wrong, because the mechanisms respond to different components.
   - If the engine only has one component (usually vertical), state the H/V assumption. For Rayleigh waves, horizontal is about 0.7× vertical in a uniform half-space; this is textbook and not sourced here.

4. **The wavemaker ratio of 2 is used outside its derivation.** It comes from gravity-wave theory with no surface tension, applied to capillary-dominated 20-40 Hz ripples. The meniscus carried by the wall adds an O(1) source, so a range of about 1-3 is more honest than 1-2.

5. **Faraday wording.** '0.3-2.5 m/s² (about 2-40 mm/s)' mixes the tongue minima with the plotted flanks. Use 'onset about 0.3-0.8 m/s² at resonances (about 2.4-8 mm/s)'. The acceleration may be peak-to-peak ('average min–max of a').

6. **The Shao anchor is not a calibration.** Do not cite it as 'consistent': the arcmin figure was miscomputed (it is 76-128 arcmin in their own model, not 20-40), and it is a resonant standing wave in a pinned-rim tank.

7. **Statuses.** The ideal-eye threshold should be an 'estimate', not 'derived', because the criterion is assumed. The meniscus height value should be 'derived', because θ is assumed.

8. **Range.** The overall 0.02-1 mm/s range is fine for shimmer. For rings it should run to a few mm/s for a casual viewer. The factor-of-3 'likely error' is optimistic, given the factor-of-10 uncertainty in the criterion that the researcher acknowledges.

9. **Mercalli.** Keeping it as context only is right. Add that 1.41 cm/s is the conversion value at MMI 4.0 (the band is about 0.65-3.1 cm/s).
missing:
1. **The negative result needs evidence that holds up.** The cited Leicester search returns 'No Results' for every query, even 'physics', so it proves nothing. Record the real search strings and databases used.
2. **Glass contact angle.** No source for water on household soda-lime glass, clean versus used. The vertical (ring) threshold scales with the meniscus height.
3. **Floor and table transfer.** No source for amplification from the ground to a table top. Suspended floors and tables often resonate at 10-30 Hz and can amplify several-fold. This matters more than most of the model's internal factors. Floor-vibration design guides were not fetched; AISC Design Guide 11 and SCI P354 are candidates to check.
4. **Pulse versus steady shaking.** The thresholds are for steady sinusoids. A footstep is a burst of a few cycles, so it cannot build up the glass's resonant edge-wave peaks; meanwhile the travelling ripple crosses the glass in 0.09-0.18 s. The model should state this.
5. **Better perceptual criterion.** The 10-arcmin 'noticeable' factor is a guess. Sources on motion and oscillation detection, and on hyperacuity (Webvision has a hyperacuity chapter), could tighten or replace it.
6. **Capillary wavemaker theory.** Hocking & Mahdmina 1991 (JFM 224) and Cocciaro, Faetti & Nobili 1991 (full text, not the abstract) would replace the gravity-only ratio of 2 for capillary ripples.
7. **Which ground component the engine supplies.** The threshold topic's PPV convention (peak component, resultant, or vector sum) needs settling, along with an H/V ratio if only vertical PPV is modelled.
8. **Optional qualitative fact.** Terwagne & Bush 2011 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.6348): small wall-driven capillary waves are 'almost invisible to the naked eye' but 'readily detected by appropriate lighting'. This supports the lighting caveat.
9. **Primary production source for the film effect.** No Lantieri interview or DVD featurette was fetched, and the cited secondary sources conflict.
verdict:
The research is careful, and nearly all quoted numbers and sentences match the re-fetched sources. I fetched 16 URLs and recomputed with my own scripts: the IAPWS table, the Mercalli wording, the ShakeMap legend, the Shao et al. quotes and figures, Karjanto, Denner, Delon, Wilson, Webvision, Accu Dyne and Film Stories all check out. The wave-scale table recomputes exactly. The recommended 0.2 mm/s survives, because the side-to-side wavemaker mechanism sets it at 10, 20 and 40 Hz.

Fix several things before use:
- **Meniscus model.** The η heuristic overstates up-and-down (concentric-ring) radiation by up to about 5× at 40 Hz. Corrected ring thresholds are about 0.5-1 mm/s, so 0.2 mm/s means 'visible shimmer', not 'Jurassic Park rings'. The page needs two numbers and a component convention.
- **Shao anchor.** The 'consistency check' is miscomputed and is in any case a resonant standing wave, so it is not a check.
- **Negative result.** The Leicester search page is non-functional, so it is not evidence.
- **Faraday range.** It quotes the tongue flanks as onset values, and the acceleration may be peak-to-peak.
- **Statuses.** The ideal-eye threshold should be 'estimate' and the meniscus height 'derived'.
- **Wavemaker ratio.** The ratio of 2 is a gravity-wave constant applied to capillary ripples.
- **Film sources.** The cited sources disagree on dashboard versus floor.

None of these overturns the headline, but the ring label, the 40 Hz value and the statuses must change.
